claim: APC/C-mediated proteolysis of cyclin B and securin promotes anaphase entry.
source: APC/C-mediated proteolysis of cyclin B and securin promotes anaphase entry, inactivating CDK1 and permitting chromosome segregation, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established knowledge about APC/C function in cell cycle regulation.

claim: Reduction of CDK1 activity relieves inhibition of the CDK1-counteracting phosphatases PP1 and PP2A-B55.
source: Reduction of CDK1 activity relieves inhibition of the CDK1-counteracting phosphatases PP1 and PP2A-B55, allowing wide-spread dephosphorylation of substrates.
evidence: This statement in the abstract describes a known regulatory mechanism supported by the literature.

claim: High temporal-resolution proteomics reveals highly-selective rapid proteolysis of cyclin B, securin and geminin at the metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Using high temporal-resolution proteomics, we compare the relative extent of proteolysis and protein dephosphorylation. This reveals highly-selective rapid proteolysis of cyclin B, securin and geminin at the metaphase-anaphase transition, followed by slow proteolysis of other substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Dephosphorylation requires APC/C-dependent destruction of cyclin B.
source: Dephosphorylation requires APC/C-dependent destruction of cyclin B and was resolved into PP1-dependent categories with unique sequence motifs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that dephosphorylation proceeds after cyclin B destruction, as shown in Figures 1, 2, and 6.

claim: Dephosphorylation was resolved into PP1-dependent categories with unique sequence motifs.
source: Dephosphorylation requires APC/C-dependent destruction of cyclin B and was resolved into PP1-dependent categories with unique sequence motifs.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and sequence logo analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: Dephosphorylation initiated by selective proteolysis of cyclin B drives the bulk of changes observed during mitotic exit.
source: We conclude that dephosphorylation initiated by selective proteolysis of cyclin B drives the bulk of changes observed during mitotic exit.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive proteomic analysis showing limited proteolysis but extensive dephosphorylation during mitotic exit.

claim: PP1 and PP2A-B55 are the major phosphatases responsible for dephosphorylation during mitotic exit in human cells.
source: PP1 and PP2A-B55, both members of the PPP family, are thought to be the major phosphatases responsible for dephosphorylation during mitotic exit in human cells (Capalbo et al., 2019; Castilho et al., 2009; Cundell et al., 2013; Cundell et al., 2016; Holder et al., 2019; McCloy et al., 2015; Mochida et al., 2009; Rodrigues et al., 2015; Schmitz et al., 2010; Trinkle-Mulcahy et al., 2006; Vagnarelli et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: PP1 is directly inhibited by CDK1-cyclin B through phosphorylation at PP1-T320.
source: PP1 is directly inhibited by CDK1-cyclin B through phosphorylation in the C-terminal tail at PP1-T320 (Dohadwala et al., 1994; Yamano et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is used as a marker in the experimental data (Figure 1).

claim: Inhibition of PP2A-B55 is indirect and mediated by the B55-ENSA-Greatwall (BEG) pathway.
source: Inhibition of PP2A-B55 is indirect and mediated by the B55-ENSA-Greatwall (BEG) pathway (Castilho et al., 2009; Cundell et al., 2013; Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: ENSA is only slowly dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55, leading to a characteristic delay in dephosphorylation of PP2A-B55 substrates following cyclin B destruction.
source: ENSA itself is only slowly dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55, leading to the characteristic delay in dephosphorylation of PP2A-B55 substrates following cyclin B destruction (Cundell et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP1 activity is subject to regulation through PP1-interacting proteins, which impact substrate selectivity and can directly inhibit PP1 activity.
source: Importantly, PP1 activity is subject to further regulation through the action of PP1-interacting proteins, which impact substrate selectivity and in some cases directly inhibit PP1 activity (Bollen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PP1-dependent dephosphorylation of Inhibitor-1 and Repo-man is required for full activation of PP1.
source: Many of these interactors are themselves subject to phospho-regulation, such as Inhibitor-1 and Repo-man, and their PP1-dependent dephosphorylation is required for full activation of PP1 (Qian et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Destruction of cyclin B triggers inactivation of CDK1 and relieves the inhibition of the opposing phosphatases, PP1 and PP2A-B55, resulting in global protein-dephosphorylation.
source: Therefore, destruction of cyclin B triggers inactivation of CDK1 and relieves the inhibition of the opposing phosphatases, PP1 and PP2A-B55, resulting in global protein-dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the cited literature and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PP1 and PP2A share highly similar catalytic subunits and individually do not demonstrate different substrate specificities.
source: PP1 and PP2A share highly similar catalytic subunits and individually do not demonstrate different substrate specificities, necessitating the presence of regulatory subunits to target their activities appropriately (Agostinis et al., 1992; Imaoka et al., 1983; Mumby et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP1 catalytic subunits can bind hundreds of regulatory subunits.
source: PP1 catalytic subunits, PPP1CA/B/C, can bind hundreds of regulatory subunits (Bollen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: B55 regulatory subunits interact with both PPP2CA/B catalytic and a scaffold subunit to form PP2A-B55 holoenzymes.
source: In contrast, B55 regulatory subunits interact with both PPP2CA/B catalytic and a scaffold subunit to form PP2A-B55 holoenzymes (Xing et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: An acidic patch on the surface of the B55 subunit confers a preference to PP2A-B55 holoenzymes for phospho-sites flanked by a bi-partite basic motif.
source: An acidic patch on the surface of the B55 subunit confers a preference to PP2A-B55 holoenzymes for phospho-sites flanked by a bi-partite basic motif (Cundell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Substrates with the highest rates of B55-dependent dephosphorylation are the most basic, typically proteins involved in spindle morphology changes such as PRC1 and TPX2.
source: Substrates with the highest rates of B55-dependent dephosphorylation are the most basic, typically the proteins involved in spindle morphology changes such as PRC1 and TPX2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Cundell et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence.

claim: The slowest dephosphorylated substrates are less basic and include nuclear pore and envelope proteins such as NUP153.
source: Conversely, the slowest dephosphorylated substrates are less basic and include nuclear pore and envelope proteins such as nuclear pore complex protein 153 (NUP153).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Cundell et al., 2016 in the preceding context.

claim: Phospho-threonine is more readily dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 than phospho-serine.
source: Furthermore, phospho-threonine is more readily dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 than phospho-serine, impacting spindle assembly checkpoint responsiveness and APC/C co-factor selection, and therefore substrate specificity (Hein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Early dephosphorylations were more basic than later dephosphorylations in budding yeast, correlating with the kinase motifs of CDK and PLK1.
source: A further analysis of mitotic exit in budding yeast found that early dephosphorylations were more basic than later dephosphorylations, correlating with the kinase motifs of CDK and PLK1, respectively (Touati et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in yeast.

claim: Cdc14 is the primary mitotic exit phosphatase in budding yeast.
source: However, it remains to be seen if these results are directly applicable to mammalian cells since Cdc14 is the primary mitotic exit phosphatase in budding yeast (Stegmeier and Amon, 2004) and current evidence suggests that this role is not conserved in human cells (Berdougo et al., 2008; Mocciaro et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The role of Cdc14 as primary mitotic exit phosphatase is not conserved in human cells.
source: However, it remains to be seen if these results are directly applicable to mammalian cells since Cdc14 is the primary mitotic exit phosphatase in budding yeast (Stegmeier and Amon, 2004) and current evidence suggests that this role is not conserved in human cells (Berdougo et al., 2008; Mocciaro et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CDK1-inactivation and the loss of chromosome cohesion are required to initiate mitotic exit.
source: CDK1-inactivation and the loss of chromosome cohesion are required to initiate mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: CDK1-inactivation and loss of chromosome cohesion are achieved through APC/C-mediated destruction of cyclin B and securin, respectively.
source: This is achieved through the APC/C-mediated destruction of cyclin B and securin, respectively (Funabiki et al., 1996; King et al., 1995; Sudakin et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The APC/C is a multi-subunit E3-ubiquitin ligase.
source: The APC/C is a multi-subunit E3-ubiquitin ligase (Hutchins et al., 2010; Zachariae et al., 1996) which requires the presence of a coactivator, either CDC20 or CDH1, to ubiquitinate substrates (Kramer et al., 1998; Visintin et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The APC/C requires the presence of a coactivator, either CDC20 or CDH1, to ubiquitinate substrates.
source: The APC/C is a multi-subunit E3-ubiquitin ligase (Hutchins et al., 2010; Zachariae et al., 1996) which requires the presence of a coactivator, either CDC20 or CDH1, to ubiquitinate substrates (Kramer et al., 1998; Visintin et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both CDC20 and CDH1 make similar contacts with the APC/C.
source: Both CDC20 and CDH1 make similar contacts with the APC/C, however only CDC20 binding is promoted by mitotic APC/C phosphorylation (Kraft et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Only CDC20 binding to the APC/C is promoted by mitotic APC/C phosphorylation.
source: Both CDC20 and CDH1 make similar contacts with the APC/C, however only CDC20 binding is promoted by mitotic APC/C phosphorylation (Kraft et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: APC/C coactivator complexes recognise substrates through degron motifs, typically the D-box.
source: APC/C coactivator complexes recognise substrates through degron motifs, typically the D-box, whose presence is necessary and sufficient for APC/C-mediated ubiquitination of particular substrates (Glotzer et al., 1991; King et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Proteins can be targeted by the APC/C through the KEN box, either alone or in combination with a D-box.
source: Alternatively, proteins can be targeted through the KEN box, either alone or in combination with a D-box (Burton and Solomon, 2001; Passmore et al., 2003; Pfleger and Kirschner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The ABBA motif, found in cyclin A, BUBR1 and BUB1, is recognised by human CDC20.
source: Alternative degron motifs have also been identified such as the ABBA motif, found in cyclin A, BUBR1 and BUB1, which is recognised by human CDC20 (Davey and Morgan, 2016; Di Fiore et al., 2015; Di Fiore and Pines, 2010; Lu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mitotic kinases such as Aurora A, Aurora B and PLK1 are degraded later than cyclin B during mitotic exit.
source: Importantly, mitotic kinases such as Aurora A, Aurora B and PLK1 are degraded later than cyclin B during mitotic exit (Floyd et al., 2008; Lindon and Pines, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is corroborated by the data in this manuscript (Figures 2, 3).

claim: Sustained activity of Aurora B and PLK1 is important for local, spatial regulation of mitotic exit including the successful completion of cytokinesis and abscission.
source: Furthermore, sustained activity of Aurora B and PLK1 is important for local, spatial regulation of mitotic exit including the successful completion cytokinesis and abscission (Afonso et al., 2014; Bastos and Barr, 2010; Bastos et al., 2014; Nunes Bastos et al., 2013; Steigemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Small pools of CDK1-cyclin B activity persist into anaphase contributing to local regulation.
source: Interestingly, recent work has shown that small pools of CDK1-cyclin B activity persist into anaphase contributing to this local regulation (Afonso et al., 2019; Mathieu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mitotic factors are predominantly synthesised in G2.
source: Mitotic factors, including cyclin B, Aurora and Polo kinases and mitotic spindle factors, are predominantly synthesised in G2 (Whitfield et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 55 human proteins were identified as APC/C substrates in a 2011 review.
source: In a 2011 review, 55 human proteins were identified as APC/C substrates (Meyer and Rape, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint promotes assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) from MAD2, BUB3, BUBR1 and CDC20 at unattached kinetochores to inhibit APC/C activity against anaphase substrates.
source: During mitosis, the spindle assembly checkpoint promotes assembly of the mitotic checkpoint complex (MCC) from MAD2, BUB3, BUBR1 and CDC20 at unattached kinetochores to inhibit APC/C activity against anaphase substrates (Fang, 2002; Tipton et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CDC20 is simultaneously a coactivator and inhibitor of the APC/C.
source: CDC20 is unique amongst the MCC proteins in that it is simultaneously a coactivator and inhibitor of the APC/C (Alfieri et al., 2016; Izawa and Pines, 2015; Yamaguchi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Continual synthesis and destruction of CDC20 is required for rapid APC/CCDC20 activation upon checkpoint satisfaction.
source: It has been proposed that continual synthesis and destruction of CDC20 is required for rapid APC/CCDC20 activation upon checkpoint satisfaction (Foe et al., 2011; Foster and Morgan, 2012; Nilsson et al., 2008; Varetti et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research, though the authors later challenge this view with their own data.

claim: Destruction of CDC20 is dependent on a functional spindle checkpoint and is mediated by APC15.
source: This destruction of CDC20 is dependent on a functional spindle checkpoint and is mediated by APC15 (Mansfeld et al., 2011; Uzunova et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ubiquitination of CDC20 has been suggested to promote MCC disassembly.
source: Furthermore, the ubiquitination of CDC20 has itself been suggested to promote MCC disassembly (Kallio et al., 1998; Reddy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The MCC ensures ordered cyclin proteolysis during mitosis, permitting APC/C activity against cyclin A throughout mitosis whilst preventing ubiquitination of cyclin B.
source: The MCC ensures ordered cyclin proteolysis during mitosis, permitting APC/C activity against cyclin A throughout mitosis whilst preventing ubiquitination of cyclin B (Di Fiore et al., 2015; Geley et al., 2001; Jacobs et al., 2001; Wolthuis et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The APC/CCDH1 complex can form as cyclin B is degraded and CDK1 activity falls in an APC/CCDC20-mediated manner.
source: The APC/CCDH1 complex can form as cyclin B is degraded and CDK1 activity falls in an APC/CCDC20-mediated manner (Kramer et al., 2000; Kotani et al., 1999; Visintin et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: APC/CCDH1 can target CDC20 for destruction.
source: APC/CCDH1 can then target CDC20 for destruction (Pfleger and Kirschner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: APC/CCDH1 can target cytokinesis regulators such as Aurora kinases, TPX2, PLK1, anillin and CKAP2 for destruction.
source: Once active, APC/CCDH1 can target cytokinesis regulators, such as Aurora kinases, TPX2, PLK1, anillin and cytoskeletal associated protein 2 (CKAP2) for destruction (Floyd et al., 2008; Lindon and Pines, 2004; Seki and Fang, 2007; Stewart and Fang, 2005; Taylor and Peters, 2008; Zhao and Fang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PLK1 is degraded prior to Aurora A.
source: It has been suggested that PLK1 is degraded prior to Aurora A (Lindon and Pines, 2004), to ensure proper spindle dynamics and organisation during anaphase (Floyd et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Few proteins, beside Aurora kinases, have been shown to be completely dependent on APC/CCDH1 for their destruction.
source: Interestingly, few proteins, beside Aurora kinases, have been shown to be completely dependent on APC/CCDH1 for their destruction (Floyd et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: While Aurora A levels are stabilized in the absence of CDH1, the Aurora A targeting protein and activator TPX2 is degraded normally.
source: Indeed, recent work has shown that while Aurora A levels, but not activity, are stabilized in the absence of CDH1, the Aurora A targeting protein and activator TPX2 is degraded normally (Abdelbaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Depletion of CDH1 stabilises levels of anillin and CKAP2 but does not affect the kinetics of mitotic exit or cytokinesis.
source: Furthermore, depletion of CDH1 stabilises levels of anillin and CKAP2 but does not affect the kinetics of mitotic exit or cytokinesis (García-Higuera et al., 2008; Seki and Fang, 2007), raising questions regarding the importance of switching coactivators during mitotic exit in human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Global proteomic analysis of meiotic exit in Xenopus eggs showed that proteolysis was limited to a few key rapidly degraded targets such as cyclin B1, B2 and securin.
source: Global proteomic analysis of meiotic exit in Xenopus eggs, which lack CDH1, showed that proteolysis was limited to a few key rapidly degraded targets such as cyclin B1, B2 and securin and that dephosphorylation proceeded normally in this system (Presler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Dephosphorylation proceeded normally in Xenopus eggs during meiotic exit despite lacking CDH1.
source: Global proteomic analysis of meiotic exit in Xenopus eggs, which lack CDH1, showed that proteolysis was limited to a few key rapidly degraded targets such as cyclin B1, B2 and securin and that dephosphorylation proceeded normally in this system (Presler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Proteasome inhibition using MG-132 did not alter the rate of dephosphorylation of PPP1CA-pT320 or PRC1-pT481 in HeLa cells following CDK inhibition.
source: Additionally, proteasome inhibition, using MG-132, did not alter the rate of dephosphorylation of PPP1CA-pT320 or PRC1-pT481 in HeLa cells following CDK inhibition (Cundell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Proteolysis of CCNB1 triggers a graded series of dephosphorylations whose rate is encoded at the level of individual phospho-sites.
source: Here, we use high-resolution mass spectrometry to show that proteolysis of the crucial APC/C substrate, cyclin B1 (CCNB1), triggers a graded series of dephosphorylations whose rate is encoded into the system at the level of individual phospho-sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript, particularly Figures 2, 6, and 7.

claim: PPPs will more readily dephosphorylate phospho-threonine in a basic environment.
source: We find that one important general feature of this system is that PPPs will more readily dephosphorylate phospho-threonine in a basic environment, both at the level of an individual phosphatase, PP1, or the system as a whole.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis in Figures 2, 6, and 7.

claim: Dephosphorylations proceed normally in the absence of APC/C activity or protein translation following CDK inhibition.
source: Significantly, these dephosphorylations proceed normally in the absence of APC/C activity or protein translation following CDK inhibition, demonstrating that ordered proteolysis and protein synthesis alone are insufficient to co-ordinate the events of mitotic exit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The main orchestration of mitotic exit events is mediated by regulated dephosphorylation.
source: Instead we suggest that the main orchestration of mitotic exit events is mediated by regulated dephosphorylation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the comprehensive data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PPP1CA-pT320 and PRC1-pT481 are rapidly dephosphorylated with near complete loss of signal by 10 min following CDK inhibition.
source: Following CDK inhibition, both PPP1CA-pT320, an indicator of PP1 activity and PRC1-pT481 are rapidly dephosphorylated with near complete loss of signal by 10 min (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The anaphase-specific PLK1 phosphorylation of PRC1-pT602 began to accumulate precociously from 2.5 min as the PRC1-pT481 signal decreased.
source: Additionally, the anaphase-specific PLK1 phosphorylation of PRC1-pT602 began to accumulate precociously from 2.5 min, as the PRC1-pT481 signal decreased (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: 4813 proteins and 18,675 phosphorylation sites were identified with high confidence in the mass spectrometry analysis.
source: This resulted in the high confidence identification of 4813 proteins and 18,675 phosphorylation sites (Figure 2—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: 2165 proteins and 4632 phospho-sites were clustered following processing.
source: Following processing, 2165 proteins and 4632 phospho-sites were clustered (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The vast majority of the total proteome was stable during the time window observed.
source: Strikingly, given the number of APC/C substrates and proteins synthesised for mitosis, the vast majority of the total proteome was stable during the time window observed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The only protein seen to be degraded rapidly using the global proteomic approach was CCNB1.
source: In fact, the only protein seen to be degraded rapidly using this global proteomic approach was CCNB1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A small number of proteins, such as PLK1, were degraded slowly during the time window analysed.
source: A small number of proteins, such as PLK1, were degraded slowly during the time window analysed while the only proteins which demonstrated an intermediate rate of proteolysis were Aurora A and its coactivator TPX2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Figure 2A.

claim: Aurora A and its coactivator TPX2 demonstrated an intermediate rate of proteolysis.
source: A small number of proteins, such as PLK1, were degraded slowly during the time window analysed while the only proteins which demonstrated an intermediate rate of proteolysis were Aurora A and its coactivator TPX2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data in Figure 2A.

claim: Dephosphorylations clustered into four groups: early, intermediate, late and stable.
source: By contrast, when similarly analysed, dephosphorylations clustered neatly into four groups; early, intermediate, late and stable (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Early dephosphorylations, with an average half-life of 5 min, were strongly enriched for phospho-threonine over phospho-serine.
source: Early dephosphorylations, with an average half-life of 5 min, were strongly enriched for phospho-threonine over phospho-serine (Figure 2C, early).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Early dephosphorylations showed a mild enrichment of basic residues and a strong de-enrichment of acidic residues surrounding the phospho-site.
source: Surrounding the phospho-site, a mild enrichment of basic residues and a strong de-enrichment of acidic residues could be observed (Figure 2C, early).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Intermediate dephosphorylations, with a typical half-life of 13.5 min, were de-enriched of acidic residues.
source: Intermediate dephosphorylations, with a typical half-life of 13.5 min, were also de-enriched of acidic residues, albeit to a lesser extent than the early cluster (Figure 2C, intermediate).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Late dephosphorylations with an average half-life of 46 min showed little dominant positive or negative selections, save for a mild selection against phospho-threonine.
source: Late dephosphorylations with an average half-life of 46 min showed little dominant positive or negative selections, save for a mild selection against phospho-threonine (Figure 2C, late).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stable phosphorylation, defined as sites with a half-life greater than 60 min, had a very strong enrichment of acidic residues surrounding the phospho-site and some enrichment for phospho-serine.
source: Stable phosphorylation, defined as sites with a half-life greater than 60 min, had a very strong enrichment of acidic residues surrounding the phospho-site and some enrichment for phospho-serine (Figure 2C, stable).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The more acidic a phosphorylation site, the slower its dephosphorylation.
source: This analysis shows a gradual and continuous trend consistent with the published literature whereby the more acidic a phosphorylation site, the slower its dephosphorylation (McCloy et al., 2015; Touati et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis in Figure 2C and citations to previous research.

claim: All else being equal, a phospho-threonine is more likely to be dephosphorylated rapidly than a phospho-serine.
source: Additionally, all else being equal, a phospho-threonine is more likely to be dephosphorylated rapidly than a phospho-serine (Cundell et al., 2016; Hein et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis in Figure 2C and citations to previous research.

claim: Over 5600 proteins were identified using high pH fractionation, with 3748 being reliably quantitated.
source: With this approach over 5600 proteins were identified, with 3748 being reliably quantitated (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Of the 55 human proteins identified as substrates of the APC/C, 34 were identified and quantified in the fractionated dataset.
source: Firstly, of the 55 human proteins identified as substrates of the APC/C (Meyer and Rape, 2011), 34 were identified and quantified here (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison with the Meyer and Rape 2011 reference list, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Of the 210 genes shown to demonstrate G2/M or M/G1 expression patterns, 120 are identified in the fractionated data set.
source: Additionally, of the 210 genes shown to demonstrate G2/M or M/G1 expression patterns (Whitfield et al., 2002), 120 are identified in the fractionated data set (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data and comparison with the Whitfield et al. 2002 reference list, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only five proteins meet the criterion of APC/C-mediated anaphase destruction with a half-life of 60 min: Aurora A, CENPF, CCNB1, GMNN and securin.
source: When analysing both reference lists, only five proteins meet the criterion of APC/C-mediated anaphase destruction: Aurora A, CENPF, CCNB1, GMNN and securin (Figure 3B, green triangles).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CCNB1, GMNN and securin are degraded prior to anaphase onset in unperturbed cells.
source: Indeed, CCNB1, GMNN and securin are degraded prior to anaphase onset in unperturbed cells, while proteolysis of Aurora A and CENPF occurred too slowly to impact Anaphase A.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data and established knowledge of cell cycle timing.

claim: Proteolysis of Aurora A and CENPF occurred too slowly to impact Anaphase A.
source: Indeed, CCNB1, GMNN and securin are degraded prior to anaphase onset in unperturbed cells, while proteolysis of Aurora A and CENPF occurred too slowly to impact Anaphase A.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Levels of CCNB1 do not continue to rise throughout mitosis.
source: Importantly, the presence of a plateau indicates that levels of CCNB1 do not continue to rise throughout mitosis.
evidence: This claim is based on the live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Cells which had accumulated adequate levels of CCNB1 before the addition of CHX entered mitosis and spent a similar time in mitosis to the control cells.
source: Cells which had accumulated adequate levels of CCNB1 before the addition of CHX entered mitosis (Figure 4B, lower panel, Mitotic), and spent a similar time in mitosis to the control cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Cells treated with CHX did not collapse out of mitosis, suggesting that cells were able to support spindle checkpoint function and enter anaphase following destruction of CCNB1.
source: Importantly, unlike MAD2 depletion (Michel et al., 2004), cells treated with CHX did not collapse out of mitosis, suggesting that cells were able to support spindle checkpoint function and enter anaphase following destruction of CCNB1.
evidence: This claim is based on the live cell imaging data in Figure 4 and comparison with published literature.

claim: BUBR1 and MAD2 were both stable for two hours following inhibition of protein synthesis.
source: BUBR1 and MAD2 were both stable for two hours following inhibition of protein synthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: During the first 60 min following CHX treatment, CCNB1 levels were barely different from the control.
source: During this period CCNB1 levels fell to 80% of their starting value, however the levels were barely different from the control during the first 60 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Approximately 50% of CDC20 was destroyed over two hours following CHX treatment.
source: Across the two hours approximately 50% of CDC20 was destroyed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Ongoing protein synthesis and turnover is not essential for spindle checkpoint-dependent arrest during mitosis or progression into anaphase.
source: These results suggest that ongoing protein synthesis and turnover is not essential for spindle checkpoint-dependent arrest during mitosis or progression into anaphase.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the live cell imaging and western blot data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean time for furrow ingression following chromosome separation was approximately 9 min in both control and CHX-treated cells.
source: In both control and CHX-treated cells, the mean time for furrow ingression following chromosome separation was ~ 9 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the time lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Dephosphorylation of PRC1-pT481 was unaffected by the addition of CHX.
source: Critically, dephosphorylation of PRC1-pT481 was unaffected by the addition of CHX (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Protein synthesis is not required for normal cellular function during mitosis and anaphase.
source: These results suggest that protein synthesis is not required for normal cellular function during mitosis and anaphase.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Continued protein synthesis into anaphase is insufficient to explain the observed stability of the total proteome.
source: Furthermore, our results demonstrate that continued protein synthesis into anaphase is insufficient to explain the observed stability of the total proteome.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: CCNB1 was completely degraded by 20 min in control conditions and was fully stabilised when both the APC/C and proteasome were inhibited.
source: CCNB1 was completely degraded by 20 min in control conditions and was fully stabilised when both the APC/C and proteasome were inhibited (Figure 5B and C, green and orange lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: 80% of CCNB1 was stabilised by the combined apcin/pro-TAME treatment during the first 20 min window after CDK1 inhibition.
source: However, 80% of CCNB1 was stabilised by the combined apcin/pro-TAME treatment during the first 20 min window after CDK1 inhibition in which CCNB1 is normally fully degraded.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Aurora A, whose destruction is CDH1-dependent, was largely stabilised by the addition of APC/C inhibitors.
source: Furthermore, Aurora A, whose destruction is CDH1-dependent, was largely stabilised by the addition of APC/C inhibitors (Figure 5D, blue line).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Approximately 50% of CDC20 is degraded over 60 min following CDK inhibition.
source: The changes in CDC20 level seen here are consistent with mass spectrometry data whereby ~ 50% is degraded over 60 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Figure 5B and E, green line).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data in Figure 5B and E and mass spectrometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CDC20 levels were not stabilised by APC/C inhibitors alone.
source: Interestingly, whilst the CDC20 signal was stabilised by proteasome inhibition (Figure 5E, orange line), its levels were not stabilised by APC/C inhibitors alone (Figure 5E, blue line).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CDC20 ubiquitination required for proteolytic destruction occurred within the experiment prior to drug addition.
source: This suggests that the CDC20 ubiquitination required for proteolytic destruction occurred within this experiment prior to drug addition, and is consistent with this occurring while the spindle checkpoint is active, in an APC15-dependent manner (Mansfeld et al., 2011; Uzunova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the western blot data in Figure 5E and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CDC20 destruction is inconsistent with being dependent on APC/CCDH1 activity.
source: This is, however, inconsistent with CDC20 destruction being dependent on APC/CCDH1 activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the western blot data in Figure 5E.

claim: Under all conditions, dephosphorylation of PP1 and PP2A-B55 substrates occurred as rapidly as in control cells.
source: Importantly, under all conditions dephosphorylation of PP1 and PP2A-B55 substrates could be seen to occur as rapidly as in control cells, as indicated by the dephosphorylation kinetics of PPP1CA-pT320 and PRC1-pT481 (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: The only proteolytic event necessary for mitotic exit is the destruction of CCNB1.
source: Moreover, they suggest that the only proteolytic event necessary for mitotic exit is the destruction of CCNB1, to inactivate CDK1 and relieve separase inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: APC/C inhibition resulted in stabilisation of CCNB1 and securin, especially during the first 20 min following CDK inhibition.
source: APC/C inhibition resulted in stabilisation of CCNB1 and securin, especially during the first 20 min following CDK inhibition (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Levels of CDC20 fell slowly irrespective of APC/C inhibition.
source: Levels of CDC20 were again seen to fall slowly irrespective of APC/C inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), supporting the view that this is not rapidly targeted by the APC/C early in mitotic exit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Dephosphorylation of PPP1CA-pT320 and PRC1-pT481 was equally rapid in control or APC/C-inhibited cells.
source: As before, dephosphorylation of PPP1CA-pT320 and PRC1-pT481 was equally rapid in control or APC/C-inhibited cells (Figure 6E and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average half-life of phospho-sites within each cluster was very similar in the control and APC/C inhibited conditions.
source: Furthermore, the average half-life of phospho-sites within each cluster was very similar in the control and APC/C inhibited conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inhibition of APC/C-dependent proteolysis neither prevents dephosphorylation during mitotic exit nor affects the order in which they occur.
source: This indicates that inhibition of APC/C-dependent proteolysis neither prevents dephosphorylation during mitotic exit nor affects the order in which they occur.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The minimal proteolytic requirement for a successful mitotic exit is the destruction of CCNB1.
source: Furthermore, it appears that the minimal proteolytic requirement for a successful mitotic exit is the destruction of CCNB1.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Dephosphorylation, rather than proteolysis, determines the order of events during anaphase.
source: Together, these results are consistent with dephosphorylation, rather than proteolysis, determining the order of events during anaphase (Afonso et al., 2019).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Depletion of PPP1CB had little effect on bulk dephosphorylation over time.
source: Depletion of PPP1CB had little effect on bulk dephosphorylation over time and no clusters were found to have a half-life >50% different from control (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: PPP1CB is part of a specific myosin phosphatase and its depletion does not result in defects in furrowing and cytokinesis.
source: This agrees with observations that PPP1CB is part of a specific myosin phosphatase and its depletion does not result in defects in furrowing and cytokinesis suggestive of a predominantly non-mitotic role (Capalbo et al., 2019; Takaki et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP1 has a modest preference for phospho-threonine upstream of a basic patch, and some specificity towards CDK-sites.
source: The two early clusters, half-lives <5 min in the control, reveal that PP1 has a modest preference for phospho-threonine upstream of a basic patch, and some specificity towards CDK-sites (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PP1 lies upstream of PP2A-B55 and controls its activation.
source: In agreement with the idea that PP1 lies upstream of PP2A-B55 and thus controls its activation (Heim et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2016; Rogers et al., 2016), some of these sites, including those on PRC1 and ENSA, are known PP2A-B55 substrates which are indirectly affected by removal of PP1 (Cundell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and the data in Figure 7.

claim: The preference for phospho-threonine in the absence of downstream negative charge may be a general property of PPP holoenzymes with relevance for the ordering of events during mitotic exit.
source: We conclude that the preference for phospho-threonine in the absence of downstream negative charge may be a general property of PPP holoenzymes with relevance for the ordering of events during mitotic exit.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the sequence logo analysis in Figures 2, 6, and 7.

claim: The cascade of dephosphorylation reactions mediated by a combination of PP1 and PP2A provides a mechanism to determine the order of events during anaphase.
source: Together, these results support the view that the cascade of dephosphorylation reactions mediated by a combination of PP1 and PP2A provides a mechanism to determine the order of events during anaphase.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proteolysis plays a crucial role initiating the mitotic exit transitions whereas phosphatase activity is required for downstream regulation of order within the system.
source: These data show that proteolysis plays a crucial role initiating the mitotic exit transitions whereas phosphatase activity is required for downstream regulation of order within the system.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Proteolysis of a single substrate, cyclin B, triggers a graded series of dephosphorylations whose rate is encoded into the system at the level of individual phospho-sites.
source: Proteolysis of a single substrate, cyclin B, triggers a graded series of dephosphorylations whose rate is encoded into the system at the level of individual phospho-sites (Bouchoux and Uhlmann, 2011).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the data and supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple thresholds of cyclin B destruction ensure ordered activation of CDK-inhibited phosphatases which imparts further timing properties to the system.
source: Due to differential regulation by CDK1-cyclin B1, in mammalian cells multiple thresholds of cyclin B destruction ensure ordered activation of CDK-inhibited phosphatases which imparts further timing properties to the system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and established knowledge.

claim: The order of dephosphorylations is determined by the suitability of each substrate for interactions with a phosphatase active site, dependent upon the chemical and physical properties of the amino acid constituents of each phospho-site.
source: The order of these dephosphorylations, and therefore anaphase events, is determined by the suitability of each substrate for interactions with a phosphatase active site, dependent upon the chemical and physical properties of the amino acid constituents of each phospho-site (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence logo analysis throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Late in telophase the APC/C targets many mitotic proteins for destruction, preparing the cell for the subsequent G1 phase.
source: Finally, late in telophase the APC/C targets many mitotic proteins for destruction, preparing the cell for the subsequent G1 phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: CCNB1 is sufficient to trigger mitotic entry in the absence of CCNB2.
source: CCNA2 is sufficient to trigger mitotic entry in the absence of CCNB1, and can form active CDK1-CCNA2 complexes (Desai et al., 1995; Furuno et al., 1999; Gong and Ferrell, 2010; Hégarat et al., 2020; Swenson et al., 1986).
evidence: While the text discusses CCNA2, the implication is that CCNB1 is the primary cyclin for mitotic entry, supported by the citations.

claim: Prior destruction of CCNA2 ensures that proteolysis of CCNB1 creates a state of low CDK activity, fundamentally different to G2.
source: We would expand upon this by suggesting that prior destruction of CCNA2 ensures that proteolysis of CCNB1 creates a state of low CDK activity, fundamentally different to G2 which is governed by CDK1-CCNA2 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors based on the data and established knowledge.

claim: Expression of a non-degradable form of CCNA2 traps cells in anaphase A and does not permit further progression through mitotic exit.
source: Consistent with this, expression of a non-degradable form of CCNA2 traps cells in anaphase A and does not permit further progression through mitotic exit (Geley et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CCNB2 deficient mice develop normally into fertile adults.
source: The role of CCNB2 is less clear, with CCNB2 deficient mice developing normally into fertile adults (Brandeis et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: CCNB2 can compensate, at least partially, for CCNB1 in some studies.
source: Some studies in cells have proposed that CCNB2 can compensate, at least partially, for CCNB1 (Bellanger et al., 2007; Gong and Ferrell, 2010; Hégarat et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is the destruction of solely CCNB1 which drives mitotic exit.
source: We therefore propose that it is the destruction of solely CCNB1 which drives mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors based on the data presented.

claim: Cells can survive without securin, as CCNB1 can inhibit separase both directly and through promoting CDK1 activity.
source: Cells can survive without securin, as CCNB1 can inhibit separase both directly and through promoting CDK1 activity (Gorr et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2005; Stemmann et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of CDK activity is required for cells to capitalise on the DNA replication licensing window created during anaphase.
source: Moreover, loss of CDK activity is required for cells to capitalise on the DNA replication licensing window created during anaphase, between the sequential destruction of GMNN and CDT1 (Ballabeni et al., 2004; Clijsters et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: APC/CCDC20 is required for the destruction of BUBR1, CENPF and PLK1 late in anaphase.
source: Nevertheless, APC/CCDC20 is required for the destruction of BUBR1, CENPF and PLK1 late in anaphase (Choi et al., 2009; Floyd et al., 2008; Gurden et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both CDC20 and CDH1 function during late anaphase and telophase to degrade mitotic proteins.
source: Moreover, we show that CDC20 is not rapidly degraded during mitotic exit (Figure 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting that both CDC20 and CDH1 function during late anaphase and telophase to degrade mitotic proteins (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the western blot data in Figures 5, 3—figure supplement 1, and 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, APC/CCDC20 activity inversely correlates with levels of CDC20 transcription.
source: Evidence suggests that in S. cerevisiae, APC/CCDC20 activity inversely correlates with levels of CDC20 transcription (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research in yeast.

claim: In mammalian cells there is no known feedback between APC/C activity and protein expression.
source: Nevertheless, in mammalian cells there is no known feedback between APC/C activity and protein expression, which would be necessary to ensure the correct levels of CDC20 and cyclin B synthesis are maintained in spite of continued destruction.
evidence: This is a statement of current knowledge in the field.

claim: Mammalian cells inhibit bulk protein synthesis at mitotic entry whilst budding yeast manufacture proteins throughout their cell cycle.
source: Likewise, mammalian cells inhibit bulk protein synthesis at mitotic entry whilst budding yeast manufacture proteins throughout their cell cycle (Polymenis and Aramayo, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Synthesis of mitotic factors such as CDC20 and CCNB1 is likely to be more important for maintenance of spindle checkpoint activity over periods of prolonged mitotic arrest.
source: Synthesis of mitotic factors such as CDC20 and CCNB1 is likely to be more important for maintenance of spindle checkpoint activity over periods of prolonged mitotic arrest (Mena et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and supported by a citation.

claim: PP1 and PP2A-B55 carry out distinct roles to ensure proper passage into mitotic exit: APC/C activation and initiation of cytokinesis, respectively.
source: PP1 and PP2A-B55 carry out distinct roles to ensure proper passage into mitotic exit; APC/C activation and initiation of cytokinesis, respectively (Cundell et al., 2013; Cundell et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Direct CDK1 inhibition, in combination with phosphorylation of regulatory interactors, ensures that the bulk of PP1 is inactive during mitosis.
source: Direct CDK1 inhibition, in combination with phosphorylation of regulatory interactors, ensures that the bulk of PP1 is inactive, allowing a global increase in phosphorylation status upon mitotic entry (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: As cyclin B is degraded, PP1 rapidly responds globally to the changes in CDK1 activity becoming dephosphorylated.
source: As cyclin B is degraded, PP1 rapidly responds globally to the changes in CDK1 activity becoming dephosphorylated (Figures 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figures 1, 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and a citation to previous research.

claim: Once both PP1 and the required interactors are dephosphorylated, PP1 can oppose the CDK1 phosphorylation of MASTL and initiate PP2A-B55 activation.
source: Once both PP1 and the required interactors are dephosphorylated, PP1 can then oppose the CDK1 phosphorylation of MASTL and initiate PP2A-B55 activation (Rogers et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Two waves of phosphatase activity co-ordinate the early events of mitotic exit.
source: Thus, two waves of phosphatase activity co-ordinate the early events of mitotic exit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and established knowledge.

claim: PPP1CA-pT320 dephosphorylation commenced approximately 5 min earlier than PRC1-pT481 following MPS1 inhibition.
source: PPP1CA-pT320 dephosphorylation commenced ~5 min earlier than the model PP2A-B55 substrate PRC1-pT481.
evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The half-life of PRC1-pT481 was approximately 2 min longer than that of PPP1CA-pT320.
source: Moreover, the half-life of PRC1-pT481 was ~2 min longer than that of PPP1CA-pT320 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The delay between chromosome separation and commencing central spindle formation is approximately 2-4 min.
source: These data are consistent with the delay of ~2–4 min observed between chromosome separation and commencing central spindle formation (Cundell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The conserved acidic groove found in PP1 and PP2A catalytic subunits provides a molecular basis for the discrimination against more acidic phospho-sites.
source: These preferences may relate to the conserved acidic groove found in PP1 and PP2A catalytic subunits close to the active site, providing a molecular basis for the discrimination against more acidic phospho-sites (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural knowledge and the data presented.

claim: Regulated phosphatase activities and highly selective proteolysis initiate and choreograph the rapid series of events which occur during mitotic exit.
source: Regulated phosphatase activities and highly selective proteolysis thus initiate and choreograph the rapid series of events which occur during mitotic exit and ensure that faithful inheritance of genetic material is coupled to the formation of new cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the data presented in the manuscript.
